paragraphs: Rabbi Yehudah HaSabar, a Tanna of a baraita.

He is mentioned once, in [Eruvin 72b](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.72b.1), where he says, “Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree about partitions,” and so on. R-Y [ר״י] said in the name of Rav, “The halakhah follows Rabbi Yehudah HaSabar.” Hyman reports that the Bach reads R’ Yehudah HaSavakh.

notes.text: The first ר״י reporter remains unidentified: the consulted Eruvin paragraph names Rav Nachman reporting Rav, while Hyman prints initials with yod. The later abbreviation clearly denotes Yehudah HaSabar. HaSavakh is the Bach reading as Hyman reports it.

The consulted ruling has [Rav Nachman speaking in Rav’s name](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.72b.6). [Tosafot](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosafot_on_Eruvin.72b.1.1) quotes Rabbeinu Chananel’s HaSavakh, and the linked [Rif](https://www.sefaria.org/Rif_Eruvin.22a.2) uses the same form. [Heilprin’s entry](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=1675&lang=en) records both names and the possible explanations of HaSavakh.

Hyman’s printed notice (vol. II, p. 615) has ר״י before “said in the name of Rav.” Eruvin 72b instead names Rav Nachman. It also specifies that the partitions on which the two schools agree reach the ceiling. Tosafot attributes HaSavakh to Rabbenu Chananel, and the Bach’s gloss on Tosafot records the form in its place-name explanation. The Bach on Rif Eruvin 22a also uses HaSavakh.
